With the recent advancement of the neural rendering algo-            queries such as the referring segmentation task, as men-
rithm [3, 5, 10, 11, 21, 27, 34, 38, 39, 43, 53, 56, 57, 60, 75],    tioned in [15]. More recently, ReferSplat [15] proposes
several primitives have been introduced to represent the             to cope with segmentation from complex queries, and fo-

eral extensions [6, 12, 69, 76] have recently emerged as             viding human-annotated observable objects’ masks and cor-
a groundbreaking technique for novel view synthesis, of-             responding detailed natural language sentence descriptions
fering an exceptional balance of visual fidelity and real-           for training. However, all the aforementioned approaches

perform the novel-view synthesis task.                               DINO, limiting the capability of dealing with arbitrary tex-

2. Related Works                                                 We start by reconstructing scenes from multi-view input
                                                                 images. To this end, we employ the recently emerged
3D scene representation with different primitives. Neu-          SVR [58], which reconstructs scenes as sparse voxel fields
ral radiance fields (NeRF) [3, 5, 10, 11, 21, 27, 34, 38, 39,    and achieves high-quality reconstruction and real-time ren-
43, 53, 56, 57, 60, 75] have established a powerful paradigm     dering. The reconstructed voxels are also suitable for ef-
for representing scenes as continuous volumetric fields, en-     ficiently assigning attributes to certain 3D locations, which
abling high-quality novel view synthesis but suffering from      our algorithm exploits. Their rendering follows the classical
slow training and rendering. To address these limitations,       volume rendering equation, which is also the one employed

Figure 2. Overview of OpenVoxel. Taking a sparse voxel model V1:N pre-trained from multi-view images I1:K and their corresponding
camera pose ξ1:K , we aim to build a voxel group field F1:N from segmentation masks M1:K obtained from SAM2. With F1:N we render
images and masks for all groups to obtain canonical captions and construct a Scene Map S recoding their position and captions. In the
Referring Query Inference stage we take a query description and image to find the ideal target group that matches the description by query
refinement and text-to-text retrieving from S, enabling complex segmentation tasks such as referring expression segmentation (RES).

by NeRF [39] and 3DGS [24]:                                              three main components: (1) Training-Free Sparse Voxel
       X                                   Y                             Grouping that groups voxels into coherent 3D instances

         i<N                                   j<i                       stores the detailed captions and 3D spatial information for
                                                              (1)        all voxel groups (Sec. 4.2), and (3) Referring Query In-
where C(r) is the rendering result for ray r, i goes through             ference to support querying and reasoning with natural lan-
an ordered list of N voxels in front of the ray, ci is the voxel         guage input from users (Sec. 4.3).
attribute (usually color) to render, αi (r) is the opacity of the
ray passing through the voxel, and finally wi (r) is the con-
tributing weight from the voxel to the rendered ray, which
is also used in our algorithm during grouping.                           4.1. Training-Free Sparse Voxel Grouping

4. Methodology                                                           Drawing inspiration from deep hough voting [48] and spa-
                                                                         tial embedding [44], our key insight is that voxels belong-
We first define the notation and problem statement of our                ing to the same object instance should cluster around a
framework. As shown in Fig. 2, given a 3D scene re-                      common 3D center position. With this motivation, we en-
constructed as N sparse voxels {Vi }N   i=1 from a set of K              code group membership of voxels as 3D spatial coordinates
multi-view images {Ii ∈ RH×W ×3 }K     i=1 with their camera             pointing to their instance centroids. These spatial embed-
poses {ξi ∈ SE(3)}K   i=1 , our goal is to assign descriptive            ding, termed as group feature, is progressively updated by
language information to these voxels to construct a scene                readily available 2D segmentation masks from foundation
map S and enable open-vocabulary reasoning from a natu-                  models like SAM2 [52]. Our update is efficiently done
ral language description D, which can be a vocabulary as in              in one training-free pass through all K views without the
3D-OVS [33] or a referring expression as in 3D-RES [15].                 lengthy gradient descent. In contrast, existing methods like
We target gradient-descent-free and latent-dimension-free                Gaussian Grouping [71] rely on gradient descent to up-
approaches to save space and time.                                       date per-primitive high-dimensional features with sequen-
    To this end, we present OpenVoxel, which consists of                 tial training processes.
